A random variable and a value that it takes are different objects.
Before the data are collected, the outcome is a random variable;
after, it is a number.
Statements about the two have different meanings.
Write them with different symbols.

Use a capital letter for the random variable
and the matching lowercase letter for a value that it takes:

- $Y$ is the random variable, such as the outcome of a coin flip before the flip;
- $y$ is one value of $Y$, such as 1 after the flip lands heads;
- $Y_i$ is the random variable for the $i$-th observation;
- $y_i$ is that observation's observed value.

State the convention where you first use the symbols.
Keep it in every later section.
Do not switch between $Y_i$ and $y_i$ for the same quantity
unless the meaning changes from "before the data" to "after the data".

::: {#exm-random-variable-vs-value}

## Writing a random variable and its value

> ❌ The probability that $y_i$ exceeds 3 is $0.2$.
>
> ✅ The probability that $Y_i$ exceeds 3 is $0.2$.

> ❌ The sample mean of the $Y_i$ is 2.4. <!-- check-term-links: allow -->
>
> ✅ The sample mean of the $y_i$ is 2.4.

A probability is a statement about a random variable.
The ❌ version of the first pair puts a fixed number
where a quantity that can vary belongs.
An observed number has no probability of exceeding 3.
The second pair has the reverse mistake.
A sample mean of 2.4 is a number computed from observed values.
The ❌ version attributes it to the random variables.
The sample mean of the random variables, $\bar{Y}$, is itself a random variable.

:::

Match the notation to the claim:

- Write $\Pr(Y \le y)$ for a probability,
  with the random variable on the left of the inequality
  and the value on the right.
- Write $\text{E}[Y]$ and $\text{Var}(Y)$ for the mean and [variance](defining-terms.qmd#def-variance-expression-and-prose)
  of a random variable,
  never $\text{E}[y]$ or $\text{Var}(y)$ for an observed value.
- Write a statistic computed from observed values with lowercase letters,
  as in $\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$,
  and the same statistic as a random variable with capitals,
  $\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$.
  The first is a number, such as 2.4.
  The second has a sampling distribution.

Name the kind of object in the words, too, not only in the symbol.
Call a random variable a "variable", such as "the output variable $\Outvar$",
and call a number a "value", such as "the input value $\predvar$" or "the observed value $\outvar$".
Do not say "fix $\predvar$" or "let $\predvar$ be fixed".
It does not say whether $\predvar$ is a variable held constant or a value you chose.
Say "choose an input value $\predvar$",
or "take the observed value $\outvar$ as given".

::: {#exm-variable-vs-value-in-words}

## Naming a variable and its value in the words

> ❌ Fix an input $\predvar$, and let $\Outvar = \truemeanf{\predvar} + \noise$.
>
> ✅ Choose an input value $\predvar$,
> and let the output variable $\Outvar = \truemeanf{\predvar} + \noise$.

The ❌ version leaves the reader to work out
that $\predvar$ is a number you choose and $\Outvar$ is random.
The ✅ version names the input as a value and the output as a variable,
which is what the symbols say.

:::

Some fields reserve capital letters for matrices,
or use the same letter for a random variable and its value.
In that case, say so where you introduce the symbols.
Add a word that tells the reader which meaning applies,
such as "the random variable $Y_i$" or "the observed value $y_i$".
